inline.s: “Subhuti, the Dharma attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor void.”

This section says little, yet its meaning is profound and all-embracing. You should know that this is what the Tathagata realized: not only can ordinary beings not fathom its height and depth, even Bodhisattvas cannot fully comprehend it. Truly there is no place where one can even open one’s mouth. How then can it be spoken of? Only as the Elder said: by understanding the meaning of what the Buddha taught. And yet the meaning is profound and all-embracing. Profound means its depth has no bottom; all-embracing means it encompasses all things. To explain it is extremely difficult. One must analyze and dissect it point by point, explaining it layer by layer; only then may one reach the bottom of it. Listeners should likewise proceed layer by layer, analyzing and dissecting point by point, making the analysis so fine that it enters the smallest detail, without the slightest vagueness. Only then, when cultivating contemplation and practice, will one not be vague but intimate and direct, and only then may results be hoped for. Otherwise one merely makes a muddled “suchness” and a fuzzy “Buddha-nature.” Moreover, one should not only analyze into the finest detail, but above all blend it all into one understanding. Yet one must first be able to analyze into the finest detail before one can blend it into one understanding. You should know that when analyzing into the finest detail, though one is analyzing meaning and principle, one is in fact already contemplating mind and nature. What has been said above is the key to hearing, contemplating, and cultivating. Do not neglect it, gentlemen.

The phrase “the Dharma attained by the Tathagata” must be grasped with care. Otherwise one will certainly entertain doubt. Let me now set up a question and answer to make this clear. Question: “Tathagata” is a designation of the virtue of the nature. Since it is spoken in terms of the nature, then it is utterly clear and utterly still; there is no such thing as a dharma, much less an attainment. Moreover, it was explained above that when the World-Honored One was with Dipankara Buddha he was then only an eighth-ground Bodhisattva, and even then he truly attained nothing from the Dharma. How then can it now be said that the Tathagata attained a Dharma? Answer: Your words are indeed reasonable. Yet to doubt this phrase on the basis of that reasoning is a great mistake. The mistake lies in looking at a single sentence without deeply savoring what follows. You should know that the words “this Dharma” in the following passage refer precisely to the Dharma that was attained. That Dharma, however, is neither real nor void. “Neither real nor void” is a phrase describing the virtue of the nature. The Dharma that was attained therefore refers precisely to the nature itself; how could it mean that there is some separate dharma? From this one may know that the phrase “the Dharma attained by the Tathagata” is like saying: one is called a Tathagata because one has realized this nature that is neither real nor void; how could it mean that there is anything else attained? Moreover, “neither real” precisely makes clear that although there is attainment, in truth nothing is attained; “neither void” precisely makes clear that it is by non-attainment that one realizes the nature. Then even to speak of attainment and of Dharma is no obstacle at all. Why so? Because Dharma refers to the nature, and attainment means realizing the nature. It does not mean that after becoming a Tathagata there is still an attainment and a Dharma. Hence no obstacle. If one misunderstands it as the Tathagata having attained a Dharma, then it would not be “neither real.” And if there were the slightest attainment, that would be attachment to dharmas; how then could one become a Tathagata? So it would also not be “neither void.” Thus one sees that the Buddha’s words are inherently perfect and fused; the point is to view the whole purport together and understand with a quiet mind. One should know it in this way. (Here the meaning of “neither real nor void” has already been stated in two ways. First, as a phrase describing the virtue of the nature: why the nature is neither real nor void will be explained below. Second, as a phrase describing the attainment of the virtue of the nature: the saying that “where there is attainment, there is no attainment” refers to this. Savor it carefully.) Not only is what the Tathagata realized neither real nor void. Consider what was said above concerning the four fruits: in every case, where there is attainment one does not attain, and only when there is nothing attained does one then attain. Then all of them are clearly neither real nor void. Hence it was said above: “All sages and saints are alike in that they differ through the unconditioned Dharma,” which precisely makes clear that they are alike in being neither real nor void (neither real nor void is neither arising nor ceasing; this will be explained below), differing only in whether theirs is partial or full. (Partial means not complete. The Small Vehicle is partial; the Bodhisattva is full. The Bodhisattva is partial; the Buddha is full.) In sum, Tathagata is a designation of the virtue of the nature; “neither real nor void” is the countenance of the virtue of the nature. The meaning of this section is that the nature realized by the Tathagata cannot be named or spoken. One may provisionally describe it for you as “neither real nor void” and no more. Why is the virtue of the nature neither real nor void? You should know that “neither real” means that arising and ceasing have ceased (ordinary feeling is emptied), and that there is no wisdom and no attainment (the sage’s understanding is also emptied); “neither void” means that quiescent extinction appears before one (the essence manifests) and that one can remove all suffering (the function manifests). In plain terms, “neither real nor void” is like saying quiescence and illumination at the same time. Quiescent, therefore neither real; illuminating, therefore not void. Not only is the Tathagata thus; even of the deluded mind of ordinary beings one may say that it too is neither real nor void. That the mind cannot be found when sought — is this not “neither real”? That a single fleeting thought contains the ten dharma-realms — is this not “neither void”? From this one may know that ordinary beings and sages share one substance. But because ordinary beings cling to the real and do not know the neither-real, they cannot become sages. The Small Vehicle again clings to the void and does not awaken to the neither-void, so it cannot become Bodhisattva. One class of Bodhisattvas can be neither real nor void, yet cannot be free of both real and void together, so they cannot become Tathagata. Yet in the end, because they share the same substance, they can turn their heads and find the shore. The Buddha said: “If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi.” Let us press forward with vigor. Let all living beings awaken quickly.

“Neither real nor void” has the same meaning as “neither arising nor ceasing.” Originally there is no arising, hence “neither real.” Now there is also no ceasing, hence “neither void.” It also has the same meaning as “existence is just emptiness, emptiness is just existence.” What is “neither real”? Because existence is emptiness. What is “neither void”? Because emptiness is existence. It also has the same meaning as “emptiness and existence at the same time,” since existence is just emptiness and emptiness is just existence, hence “emptiness and existence at the same time.” That is why the meanings are said to be the same. To speak thoroughly: “emptiness and existence at the same time” means that both emptiness and existence cannot be spoken of. “Neither real nor void” means that both real and void are dispelled. The dispelling of both real and void is precisely what the Heart Sutra means by “because of non-attainment, Bodhisattvas rely on this and attain ultimate nirvana, and all Buddhas rely on this and attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” Hence it is said: “The Dharma attained by the Tathagata — this Dharma is neither real nor void.” This phrase makes clear the nature realized by the Tathagata, and this nature can be spoken of neither as real nor as void. Why so? Real and void are like emptiness and existence. That emptiness and existence cannot be spoken of is quiescence and illumination at the same time. Quiescence and illumination at the same time is precisely supreme perfect enlightenment; this is what is meant by Tathagata. Above, I first set forth “neither real nor void” in parallel, in order to make clear that there is essence and there is function. Now I speak of it thoroughly, in order to make clear that essence is the root of function, and that only on attaining essence can one raise up function. Both layers of principle should be thoroughly understood. Because having essence necessarily means having function, this sutra both causes one not to attach and causes one not to destroy. Students must in this way attach to neither extreme. Because attaining essence is what raises up function, this sutra causes emptiness upon emptiness. Students must in this way transcend all appearances, emptying all the way to the end.

You should know that all the meanings taught since the beginning of this sutra are the meaning of “neither real nor void.” Why so? Because whatever is spoken is “thus-spoken.” Let me now cite a few phrases to make this clear; the rest may be inferred by analogy. For instance, where it says “all appearances are no-appearances,” “appearances are all delusive,” “neither graspable nor speakable,” “Dharma and non-Dharma are both non-existent,” and the like — all statements of the “then it is not” type are spoken according to the meaning of neither real. Where it says “this is named all Buddhas,” “then one sees the Tathagata,” “all Buddhas and their Dharmas come forth from this sutra,” and the like — all statements of the “this is named” type are spoken according to the meaning of neither void. In sum, knowing “neither real,” one knows that the nature is originally empty and quiescent, and so must sweep away emotional attachments; knowing “neither void,” one knows that cause and effect are thus — just as they are — and so should abide as taught. Why so? Because since the Tathagata realized it thus, Bodhisattvas must cultivate it thus. Thus the obtaining of this one section adds luster to all the meanings explained above. Not only that: the five statements of the previous section are all the more proven by this section. Above it was said “thus-spoken,” meaning spoken in accordance with what was realized. What then was realized? Now it is said: neither real nor void. “Neither real nor void” is the meaning of “no-appearance and yet not no-appearance,” hence it is called true speech. It is also the meaning that both appearance and non-appearance are absent, hence it is called truthful speech. Truthful speech accords in every way with what was realized, and it is manifestly not deceitful speech and not different speech.

Though “neither real nor void” is stated in parallel, the World-Honored One’s intention in saying it truly rests on the two “neithers,” teaching people that they should contemplate thoroughly and dispel both real and void. For what the Tathagata attained is indeed neither real nor void; yet “neither real nor void” is in fact obtained by dispelling both real and void. If one preserves a “neither real nor void,” that is attachment to dharmas; how then could one be neither real nor void? Therefore one must dispel and dispel again before one can realize the essence of the nature, which is empty and quiescent.

How then should a student set to work? You should know that the World-Honored One’s saying this teaches people to accomplish the neither-void by means of the neither-real. This is the skillful means for setting to work at dispelling both real and void. Why so? “Neither real” means non-attachment. Attachment means congealing and binding, and congealing is the meaning of “real.” Whether an object be real or void, once there is attachment, even the void becomes real. If one attaches to nothing at all, then both real and void are dispelled. This meaning can be seen clearly by looking at the surrounding text. The text above says: “When the mind of faith is pure, then true appearance is produced.” This is a fine gloss on neither real nor void. A pure mind is neither real; the production of true appearance is neither void. And since the production of true appearance comes from the purity of the mind, it is clear that the neither-void must be accomplished through the neither-real. Hence it was said above: “Transcending all appearances, one is named a Buddha.” And again: “One should generate the mind transcending all appearances; one should practice giving without abiding in either emptiness or existence.” Hence the text below says: “Giving while abiding in dharmas is like a person entering darkness; giving without abiding is like the sunlight shining.” And even the final verse bids one contemplate all as a dream, an illusion, and so on. Hence the whole purport of this sutra lies in “should abide in nothing whatsoever.” The World-Honored One’s intention in saying this is therefore to cause the fruit of neither-void to be accomplished by the contemplation of neither-real — is this not as clear as if held up to the light?

The contemplation of neither-real is precisely what is spoken of at the very end: contemplating all dharmas as a dream, an illusion, and so forth. Always practicing this contemplation, the clinging mind is dispelled of itself. This is the general and essential contemplation that breaks through all ordinary feelings, and one must never be separated from it even for a moment. You should know that the contemplation of dream-likeness and the rest is placed at the end because it is used to sum up the whole sutra; then it is clear that this contemplation should be practiced everywhere throughout the sutra. How then can one be bound by a rigid sequence and fail to explain it here?

Why explain it here? Because the text here is convenient and this opportunity must not be missed. Moreover, this general and essential contemplation must be stated here, and there are three further important reasons. Let me now set them out in order: (1) This is precisely the passage that makes clear what is true, and it comes directly in succession to the meaning of generating the mind without abiding and giving without abiding. And immediately following it, the text speaks at length of the fault of abiding in dharmas and the merit of not abiding. One can see that this place is precisely the linking passage between what precedes and what follows. If the meaning of non-attachment were not pointed out here, it could not serve as that link. Why so? Because it would not be connected with the meaning of non-abiding made clear above and below. (2) Moreover, since what is said here is a statement of his own realization, one cannot but point out the method of cultivation as well. Why so? The World-Honored One’s purpose in making clear that his own realization is such a fruit is to cause students to cultivate such a cause. If then one stated only the parallel meaning and did not state this meaning, how would students set to work? (3) The purpose in speaking of self-realization is not only as stated above. It is to enable those who hear the Dharma to understand clearly that everything taught in the whole sutra is a self-realization such as this — realized and confirmed, by no means a mere ideal. Therefore one need not be startled, doubtful, or afraid; therefore one must not fail to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. Therefore to uphold and teach even a four-line verse brings immeasurable merit, surpassing the giving of bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This is the greatest purpose of the World-Honored One’s speaking of self-realization. If then there were only the parallel meaning and not the thorough meaning (in other words, the meaning that by the neither-real one accomplishes the neither-void, which precisely shows students the method of practice), then listeners would know only the state of self-realization and still not know the method of self-realization; how then could it thoroughly remove people’s doubts?

Viewing all the various meanings set out above in sum, it is clear that the World-Honored One’s intention in saying this was to cause people both to know the state of his self-realization and to know the method of his self-realization. How then can those who hear the Dharma fail to receive and understand it in this way, and how can those who teach the Dharma fail to expound it in this way?

Yet this meaning, unless savored with a deep mind, will certainly be overlooked. When it was said above that the flavor of the meaning is profound and all-embracing, hard to explain and hard to understand, it was precisely this that was meant. Someone may say: “Contemplating in this way, need one not fear falling into one-sided emptiness?” The answer is: this is a plausible-sounding but false statement. You should know that cultivation of contemplation must be thorough. If it is not thorough, how can clinging be dispelled, how can appearances be transcended? Moreover, both the preceding and the following text set giving alongside it, so contemplation and practice advance together; what one-sided emptiness could there be? Besides, the World-Honored One’s sudden utterance of this meaning within the linking passage above and below is precisely to clarify the reason why, in the surrounding text, one should transcend appearances and should not abide in emptiness or existence. It makes one know that it is for this that one must transcend appearances and not abide, in order to practice giving. How can one transcend, how can one not abide? The method is thus. This is precisely where the crucial hinge of the surrounding text lies. So to say this is precisely to accomplish his original vow to practice giving widely and benefit all beings; it is by no means merely to cause this contemplation to be practiced. What fear of one-sided emptiness could there be?

Viewing what has been said above, apart from the various meanings that weave this sutra together with other sutras, one may know that the Buddha’s saying of this one phrase “neither real nor void” has three most important meanings: (1) it describes the virtue of the nature; (2) it describes how the virtue of the nature is attained; (3) it describes how the virtue of the nature is cultivated. Principle and practice, nature and cultivation, cause and effect — nothing is left out. Hence this one phrase not only encompasses without remainder the principles taught in this sutra, but also encompasses without remainder all the Buddhadharma of both the Small and the Great Vehicles. Why so? Because all sages and saints differ through the unconditioned Dharma, and “neither real nor void” is precisely what is called the unconditioned Dharma.

Not only that. All the aspects of ordinary beings’ minds, all the aspects of worldly dharmas, and all the aspects of causal dharmas are likewise encompassed without remainder. For all these aspects are existence just as emptiness and emptiness just as existence; hence they are all neither real nor void. This is precisely what the Lotus Sutra calls “such appearance, such nature, such essence, such power, such activity, such cause, such condition, such fruit, such recompense, such ultimate equality from beginning to end.” This is what is called the true appearance of all dharmas. Hence this one phrase is truly the seal of the Great Vehicle Dharma. A dharma-seal means that every single dharma can be verified by this meaning, and none can fall outside its scope. Therefore it is said that its depth has no bottom and that it encompasses all things.
3. (B) Explained again by way of simile. This is in two parts: (C) first, the simile of the fault of abiding in dharmas; next, the simile of the merit of not abiding.
(C) First, the simile of the fault of abiding in dharmas.
“Subhuti, if a Bodhisattva’s mind abides in dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness, and he sees nothing.”

This section makes clear that clinging to the real renders the merit of giving wholly void; it is precisely the reverse side of “neither real nor void.” Viewing the meaning of the two sections that follow, one is all the more able to prove that the phrase “neither real nor void” is not only spoken to make clear the state that is realized, but truly also spoken to make clear the cultivation by which it is realized. The word “dharma” here is the dharma of “one should not abide in dharmas” at the beginning of the sutra; it means all dharmas. All dharmas are none other than object, practice, and fruit. Object means the realm: the five aggregates, the six faculties, the six dusts, and so on. Practice means cultivation: the six pāramitās and so on. Fruit means the stages of fruit: the abiding, practice, dedication, and ground stages, up to supreme bodhi, and also including karmic rewards such as blessings, marks and excellences, supernormal powers, and wondrous functions. Yet as for the practices of the six pāramitās and the like, they already include object and fruit. For to practice the six pāramitās while thinking oneself able to practice — this is abiding in practice. To practice them while having thoughts of fame and the like is abiding in object. To practice them while the mind harbors a single thing attained is abiding in fruit. Whatever kind of thing the mind abides in, it is abiding in dharmas. The word “dharma” here need not include non-dharmas, because since the sutra text bases its teaching on the practice of giving, non-dharmas are already not grasped. You should know that dharmas such as the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices arise only through the confluence of causes and conditions. Since they are dharmas arisen from conditions, one may see that their very substance is empty; they are not real. Yet by practicing these dharmas of the six pāramitās one gains benefit for self and others; they are not void. Therefore the Bodhisattva should neither abandon the affairs of the six pāramitās and do nothing, falling into voidness, nor harbor attachment to the marks of the six pāramitās, clinging to the real. Clinging to the real, the mind abides in dharmas! It was said above: “If the mind abides, then it does not abide.” Hence the fault of entering darkness. Darkness means seeing nothing at all; it says that one is still within the shell of ignorance, and that not only can the light of the nature not appear. Yongjia said: “Giving attached to marks produces heavenly blessings, but draws a future life of discontent.” For one who does not know to contemplate emptiness will necessarily follow circumstances and turn; after being born in heaven, one will certainly fall. Hence it is said that this section makes clear that clinging to the real renders the merit wholly void.

Entering darkness is a simile for turning one’s back on enlightenment. Since there is attachment to dharmas, one turns one’s back on enlightenment. Enlightenment means brightness; turning one’s back on it is ignorance. Hence “entering darkness.” “Sees nothing” is a simile for not seeing the nature. It was said above: “If one sees all appearances as no-appearances, then one sees the Tathagata.” Now, not knowing the principle that what arises from conditions is just empty, one clings to it as real and grasps the marks of dharmas; how could one see the nature? Hence “sees nothing.” Nothing is said about having eyes or not having eyes because this secretly indicates that such a person’s eye of the Way is not yet opened and his ignorance not yet broken, so that having eyes is the same as having none; hence nothing is said. For because this person’s view is unclear, though he studies the Great Vehicle and practices giving, it is blind practice (entering darkness) and must produce heavy obstruction (seeing nothing); hence the simile of entering darkness and seeing nothing. You should know that if a student of Buddhism does not open the eye of the Way, he is bound to mix worldly feelings and vulgar views into everything; not only will the six pāramitās be poorly practiced, he will certainly increase his pride, vie in greed and anger, and instead throw the Buddhadharma into confusion, practicing it in a way neither fish nor fowl, arousing people’s doubt and slander. He will simply see nothing at all of the principles of the Buddhadharma, and not merely fail to see the nature. Such is the fault of grasping dharmas as real; we should sternly guard against it.
(C) Next, the simile of the merit of not abiding.
“If a Bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person who has eyes, with the sunlight shining, seeing all kinds of forms.”

This section makes clear that one knows dharmas are not real, and therefore does not abide or attach. Then the merit of giving can be not void. This is precisely what is said to expound the meaning that by the neither-real one accomplishes the neither-void, so that one may know that whoever wishes to attain what I have attained should be like this person. Such exposition of meaning is utterly clear; such instruction is utterly intimate; such exhortation to faith is utterly earnest.

“Having eyes” is a simile for the eye of the Way. “Sunlight” is a simile for the Buddha’s wisdom, and also refers to this sutra, because everything spoken in the sutra is the meaning of the Buddha’s great wisdom-light. “Seeing” is a simile for seeing the nature. “All kinds of forms” is a simile for the pure virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that the nature inherently possesses. The meaning is that one who gives while abiding in dharmas, because of clinging, produces obstruction; how could he awaken to and see the original nature? If one can keep the mind from abiding in dharmas (neither real) and yet diligently practice giving (neither void), then such a person’s eye of the Way is clear and penetrating (having eyes), and emptiness and existence are both transcended (real and void both dispelled). He is truly one who can rely on the prajñā of words to raise up the prajñā of contemplation. Then, roaming within the radiance of the Buddha-sun (the sunlight shining), he will surely come to see thoroughly the emptiness that accords with reality (neither real) and the non-emptiness that accords with reality (neither void), possessing in full the nature of the three greatnesses of essence, mark, and function (seeing all kinds of forms), even as the Buddha attained them. How could his merit be conceived! And this immediately gives rise to the section below on accomplishing immeasurable and boundless merit. This is spoken in terms of the parallel meaning of neither real nor void. If one speaks in terms of the thorough meaning in which real and void are both dispelled, then when the mind does not abide in dharmas the mind is empty — that is neither real. When the mind is empty and neither real, then the opposed marks of self, person, existence, and non-existence all depart — this is what is called the dispelling of both real and void. If one can be thus, then it is like the sunlight shining and seeing all kinds of forms — that is neither void. That by the neither-real one accomplishes the neither-void — is this not clearly shown?

“Eyes” and “sun” may also serve as similes for the practitioner’s right wisdom. “Having eyes” means the right wisdom is opened. Once the right wisdom is opened, it can break ignorance; hence “the sunlight shining.” As ignorance is broken part by part, so part by part there appear the pure virtues of the nature, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges; hence “seeing all kinds of forms.”

If giving while abiding in dharmas is still like a person entering darkness, then what state must one enter who abides and attaches to objects such as the faculties and dusts and does not practice giving? It is unbearable to imagine! Let me now set out in three classes those who do not practice the six pāramitās of giving and the rest. What was said above is one class. If the mind abides in getting good karmic rewards and yet is unwilling to give — what a fool! This is another class. There are those who abide in nothing at all as regards the faculties and dusts and yet also do not practice giving — the so-called ones who cultivate only themselves. Judged by worldly standards, roaming free beyond things, they are not at all bad; but measured by Buddhadharma, they abide in non-dharmas and are still attached to dharmas. They too are people who enter darkness and see nothing. This is yet another class.

If the mind abides in giving and yet does not practice giving, there is no such person in the world. For there is no principle by which one does not practice giving and yet grasps at giving. If one does not abide in practice or fruit and yet does not practice giving, then it is clear that one’s mind abides in the faculties and dusts, and such a one falls into the same class as the first. What the views and prospects of such people are, one may infer from the meaning made clear in these two sections; hence the World-Honored One did not speak of it.

Above, the two sections of the preceding text having been summed up, the essential meanings taught since the beginning of the sutra were expounded and blended into one whole. Then followed the two sections on what is true, proving that all his words and all his dharma-gates are nothing but true, because they are all spoken in accordance with the Dharma he realized. And then followed these two sections of simile, further clarifying the state of the realized neither real nor void and pointing out the cultivation by which it is realized. The chapters and sentences before and after are exceedingly well woven together, unfolding the meaning and principle with repeated thoroughness. Not only are the essential meanings in the summary — generating the mind while transcending appearances, the principle that abiding means not abiding, giving without abiding in forms, and so on — rendered doubly vivid, they also cast a reflected light back upon the passage at the beginning of the sutra about the Bodhisattva practicing giving without abiding in dharmas, making it more complete. For the beginning of the sutra made clear only the merit of giving without abiding, while here it also makes clear the fault of giving while abiding in dharmas; hence it is more complete. Moreover, after the summary these two sections come as a final ripple. Even judged merely as writing, it is like a dragon flicking its tail and the whole body coming alive; truly the prajñā of words. All the meanings of the sutra having thus been gathered in tightly, the text below concludes by attributing merit to upholding the sutra, in order to exhort.
3. (I) Conclusion.

“Subhuti, in future ages, if there are good men and good women who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathagata, by his Buddha-wisdom, will fully know such people and fully see such people, and they will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.”

This is the third section within the Tathagata’s confirmation and exposition. The first, the section of confirmation, confirms the Elder’s statement that to believe, understand, receive, and uphold this sutra is the foremost and most rare. The second, the section of exposition, clarifies for those who are frightened by prajñā and stand in awe of it, unable to believe, understand, receive, and uphold, that the emptiness of prajñā is the emptiness of both emptiness and existence. It accordingly blends together the essential meanings already taught and unfolds the reason for “should abide in nothing whatsoever.” It further makes clear that such teachings and such a Dharma are all the Tathagata’s own realization, just so, and are nothing but true, not deceitful, not different. Therefore one who does not understand the purport of non-abiding, though practicing the six pāramitās, finds ignorance hard to break — like a person entering darkness. One who understands the purport of non-abiding and practices the six pāramitās thereby will surely break ignorance — like the bright sun shining. Repeated and thorough, no meaning is left unilluminated. Hence this third section concludes by attributing merit to receiving and upholding this sutra, and also reflects back upon the meaning that transcending appearances is what makes one a Buddha. (Immeasurable and boundless merit has the same meaning as “then one is named all Buddhas.”) The purport of the first half of the sutra may be said to be concluded here with the utmost completeness and roundness; hence it is titled “Conclusion.” Conclusion means the meaning of completing and perfecting, and also the meaning of bringing the fruit to accomplishment.

“In future ages” refers generally to the time after the Buddha. The reason for not speaking of the present but raising up later ages is the intention that this sutra be propagated from one to another without being cut off, so that its benefit be endless. It also reflects back upon the earlier phrase “in the last five hundred years”: that in an age of firm contention one can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra shows how deep one’s roots from former lives must be. Therefore such people receive the Buddha’s protective mindfulness and all accomplish it. The word “can” precisely shows that they stand out from the crowd and are exceedingly rare. Because at a time when people seldom can, they nonetheless can, therefore they all attain what the Buddha attained.

“Receive” means to take in the purport of the meaning; that is, to understand. “Uphold” means to cultivate and maintain, that is, to practice in accordance with the Dharma. It also means to hold fast, that is, to keep it in the heart without losing it. Since one can practice in accordance with the Dharma, one will surely benefit all living beings by practicing giving. Hence although it is not explicitly said here that one widely explains it to others, that meaning is already included.

“Receiving” belongs to the wisdom of reflection; “upholding” belongs to the wisdom of cultivation; “reading and reciting” belong to the wisdom of hearing. To read by the text is “reading”; to recall and think is “reciting.” The reason “receive and uphold” is spoken first has three meanings: (1) Receiving and upholding is the deeper level, hence it is listed first; reading and reciting is the shallower level, hence it is listed next. This is spoken with two kinds of people in mind. Yet to receive and uphold, one must first read and recite. If one can truly read and recite, then receiving and upholding become possible. Hence all accomplish it. (2) Having received and upheld, one still reads and recites; this is spoken of a single person. With the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation complete, and with diligence unremitting to this degree, how could one fail to accomplish it? (3) The great section that unfolds non-abiding was spoken with the intention that hearers might thereby open their understanding. Hence this section on accomplishing the wisdom of understanding concludes by returning to understanding. “Receiving” is understanding. And the great concluding section that then most fully displays the sutra’s merit likewise speaks first of receiving and upholding. All of this makes clear that one has opened a perfect understanding, so that one’s faith is perfect faith and one’s upholding is perfect upholding. That one is known and seen by the Buddha’s wisdom and attains accomplishment depends chiefly on this. “The Tathagata, by his Buddha-wisdom, will fully know such people and fully see such people”: “by” is passive in force and is read in the departing tone. This sentence, spoken in terms of actual matters, has two meanings. (1) Wisdom is the meaning of light; knowing and seeing is the meaning of protective mindfulness. It says that such a person deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent and receives the Buddha’s empowering grace. (2) It says that such a person’s merit is known only to the Buddha; apart from Buddha-wisdom, no one else can fully know and fully see it. In sum, if a person can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then in terms of principle, his ignorance receives the perfuming of suchness (the Tathagata), and his knowing and seeing receive the perfuming of Buddha-wisdom (fully knowing and fully seeing by Buddha-wisdom). Hence in terms of matters, all such people receive the empowering grace of the Buddha Tathagata and all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit. And the words “fully know” and “fully see” show that their accomplishment is certain.

“They will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit” precisely reflects back upon the earlier statements: “you should know that such a person is most rare,” “you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost, most rare Dharma,” and the like. “They will all accomplish” means that whether monk or lay, man or woman, whoever can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra will without exception accomplish in this way. Even one who does not understand the meaning but can merely read and recite will surely attain it. Hence “all accomplish.” Why so? Because if one truly has genuine faith and reads and recites with utmost sincerity, though at first one does not understand, afterward one will surely open to understanding. Why is that? Because the seed of prajñā has been planted, and having received the Buddha’s gathering in, one’s wisdom will surely be opened. Benefiting living beings is merit; nurturing bodhi is virtue. The two words “merit and virtue” refer to saving oneself and saving others and to perpetuating the Buddha-seed; hence “immeasurable and boundless.” Why so? “Immeasurable” is spoken vertically: enduring and constant through ten thousand kalpas. “Boundless” is spoken horizontally: pervading the dharma-realm without limit. This is the state of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, whose dharma-body abides forever and whose wondrous response has no fixed direction. To say now that they all accomplish such merit makes clear that they all come to be Bodhisattvas and even to become Buddhas. In sum, this exhorts people that they must receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and thereby awaken to their own mind-nature, which is neither real nor void, far removed from the two extremes. Having made the whole nature the ground of cultivation, they will perfect the whole cultivation and realize the nature.

blocks.text: Chapter Fifteen: The Merit of Upholding the Sutra

inline.s: 5. (H) Most fully displaying the sutra’s merit. This is in four parts: (I) first, displaying it in terms of producing merit; next, displaying it in terms of erasing offenses; third, displaying it in terms of honoring Buddhas; fourth, concluding the sutra’s merit. (I) The first is again in two parts: (J) first, setting up a simile; next, displaying the surpassing.
(J) First, setting up a simile.

“Subhuti, if there are good men and good women who in the first period of the day give their bodies in number equal to the sands of the Ganges; in the middle period of the day again give their bodies in number equal to the sands of the Ganges; in the last period of the day also give their bodies in number equal to the sands of the Ganges — thus for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas giving their bodies.”

This fifth great section, most fully displaying the sutra’s merit, is the last section that unfolds non-abiding in order to open understanding; it is not only the summary of that unfolding and opening, but also the summary of the first half of the sutra. Its thread of language, moreover, continues directly from the text above. For it was said above that those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit. Why can they accomplish it thus? Hence the sutra’s merit is most fully displayed to prove it. Nevertheless, since this great section is the summary of the first half, and three comparisons have already been made above, the reason he speaks of it again to display it to the utmost is truly that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable. Though three comparisons were made above, words still did not exhaust the meaning. Hence now, taking advantage of the textual convenience above, he expounds it thoroughly once more. It is merely occasioned by the text above; it is not solely for the sake of the text above.

You should know that displaying the sutra’s merit is displaying the right wisdom of prajñā. This wisdom is the Buddha-wisdom, the so-called supreme perfect enlightenment, which our World-Honored One attained through kalpas of diligent and arduous cultivation for the sake of living beings. It is precisely the Dharma of neither real nor void spoken above. Now he sets out this Dharma entirely and makes it into this sutra: to show those who have not seen the nature a true and exact map; to serve as a compass guiding living beings to the other shore; to tell people from his own experience, so that they may have something to follow. For he pities all living beings who, from beginningless time, have been darkly unaware and long entangled in affliction — some because their obstruction is heavy do not hear the Buddhadharma, others though they hear it do not grasp the essentials of the Dharma. Then former obstruction is not removed and later obstruction arises again: the so-called seeking medicine because of illness, and then the medicine itself becoming an illness. They sit in the black mountain of ghost caves, like a person entering darkness and seeing nothing — what end is there? Therefore he distilled the meaning of prajñā spoken in the previous eight assemblies and further taught this sutra. Truly every sentence transmits the mind, every word seizes the essential. It can cause living beings to open their initial enlightenment, unite with the original enlightenment, and accomplish great enlightenment. If one can truly believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, then one is like a person who has eyes, with the sunlight shining, seeing all kinds of forms. And he plainly tells them: all Buddhas and the Dharma of supreme perfect enlightenment come forth from this sutra. Then one may know that this sutra is the family treasure handed down from Buddha to Buddha. Because our World-Honored One urgently wished to transmit the family treasure and urgently wished all living beings to know the greatness of this sutra’s benefit, which is inconceivable, he therefore again and again most fully extolled this sutra’s merit, so that hearers might give rise to the thought of how hard it is to encounter, give rise to joy, strive to read and recite, believe, understand, receive, and uphold, and all accomplish the foremost and most rare. This is the greatest purpose of most fully displaying the sutra’s merit.

In displaying the sutra’s merit, he first displays the surpassing merit it can produce. If no simile is set up, one cannot show how surpassing it is. Hence he provisionally sets up the merit of an extremely great giving as the premise for later displaying the surpassing; hence “setting up a simile.” The first, middle, and last periods of the day divide one day into three, like our saying morning, noon, and afternoon. The sands of the Ganges are extremely fine and extremely numerous, beyond counting. “Kalpa” is the Sanskrit kalpa, meaning an extremely long time. Here it is not merely one kalpa but hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. And not merely hundreds of thousands of millions, but immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: an incalculable number of incalculable periods makes one “incalculable turn”; an incalculable number of incalculable turns makes one “immeasurable.” An incalculable period is already an extremely long and extremely numerous number beyond calculation; and this number beyond calculation is multiplied again and again to make the immeasurable — how could there be any number to speak of! Thus “immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas” is merely to say countless kalpas. To give one body and life each day is already beyond what ordinary beings can do. How much more, three times a day, and at each time not merely one body and life but bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, beyond counting. And how much more, not for one day, one year, or one kalpa, but throughout countless kalpas, three times a day, giving bodies and lives beyond counting. The duration is exceedingly long, the giving exceedingly heavy, the practice and vows exceedingly firm. This is the Bodhisattva’s gate of practice. How could the greatness of his merit be reckoned in numbers? And yet it does not equal that of one who hears this sutra and gives rise to faith. Why? This principle is explained in detail below.

(J) Next, displaying the surpassing. This is in three parts: (K) first, a general indication in terms of merit; next, selecting the essential and explaining separately; third, concluding by displaying the sutra’s supremacy. (K) The first is again in two parts: (L) first, that hearing with faith already surpasses; next, that upholding and teaching surpasses still more.
(L) First, that hearing with faith already surpasses.
“If again there be a person who hears this sutra and whose faith does not turn back, his merit surpasses that.”

“Not turning back” means not going against. Hearing this sutra and deeply believing that one cannot but practice in accordance with it, one then arouses the great mind to practice each thing in accordance with the Dharma: this is faith that does not turn back. It is the faith that has resolved to set out in practice. Though only faith is spoken of here, deep understanding is included. Without deep understanding one could never arouse this faith that does not turn back. This mind being first aroused is of course not equal to having already set out in practice, as below. Yet setting out in practice is in fact rooted in the resolve of this determined mind. Hence at the very moment the mind is aroused, its merit already surpasses that of the Bodhisattva who for long kalpas gives countless bodies and lives. The word “merit” here refers precisely to the words below: bearing the Tathagata, surely attaining bodhi, with a karmic reward inconceivable. Hence it cannot be matched by other merits.
(L) Next, that upholding and teaching surpasses still more.
“How much more, then, writing it out, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it, and explaining it to others.”

That the mere arousing of the mind already surpasses is precisely because of the resolve to set out in practice. Then after one has already set out in practice, one’s merit is still greater — this goes without saying. “How much more” displays that greater superiority. “Writing it out” is for wide dissemination. In ancient times there were no printed editions; it depended entirely on copying for transmission, hence it is spoken only of writing. Today, if one resolves to propagate this sutra, then whether by woodblock, lithograph, or lead type, the merit is the same as writing it; one need not necessarily write it out. That writing is mentioned first makes clear that one forms the resolve in accordance with the Dharma, first wishing to save beings, and first wishing to save them by means of this sutra; and it further makes clear that this resolve is itself the perpetuation of the Buddha-seed. Receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting, though they seem to be saving oneself, in fact also save others. For receiving and upholding is understanding and practice advancing together, and what is practiced is none other than the three kinds of giving free of appearances. The three kinds of giving free of appearances are precisely for the benefit of all living beings. Reading and reciting likewise serve to perfume excellent understanding and increase excellent practice; they are not for anything else. Explaining it to others is practicing the gift of Dharma to benefit beings. This sutra is exceedingly profound; to resolve to dissect and explain it for beings without error, delighting in teaching without obstruction, so that hearers come to understand the purport and arouse the mind of faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding — this is the meaning. The reason this sentence is placed last is that one who cannot receive, uphold, read, and recite has no way to explain it to others. Taken together, this says that such a person can both spread this sutra to benefit beings, and practice in accordance with the Dharma to benefit beings, and still more widely perform the gift of Dharma to benefit beings; which fully proves that his faith truly does not turn back. Hence at the very moment this mind is first aroused, he already surpasses the Bodhisattva who for many kalpas gives countless bodies and lives.

The reason why he surpasses, the World-Honored One states himself below: namely, that he surpasses in all three — teaching and meaning, causal arising, and bearing. The meaning is given below, but there is no harm in stating its essentials now, so as to make the whole coherent. This sutra is an utterly perfect and sudden dharma-gate; hence the teaching and meaning surpass. It was spoken for those of perfect and sudden capacity, to keep the Buddha-seed unbroken; hence the causal arising surpasses. As for bearing: consider that this person’s faith does not turn back — that is, the capacity and the teaching mesh; only one whose prajñā-seed is deep could manage it; hence his wisdom surpasses. Writing it out, receiving and upholding it, and even explaining it — this is precisely not cutting off the Buddha-seed; hence his compassion, his vows, and his practice all surpass. Compassion, wisdom, practice, and vows being complete one by one, he can bear the Tathagata; this is what bearing surpasses means. As for that Bodhisattva who for long kalpas gives body and life, though he can do what is hard to do and his practice and vows are firm, yet if he does not possess the right wisdom of prajñā he can only become a Bodhisattva of the five supernormal powers, and in the end cannot unite principle and wisdom, attain the penetration of the extinction of outflows, and realize the fruit of ultimate enlightenment. This is his first inferiority. Since he does not possess the right wisdom of prajñā, neither self nor others can reach the far shore of nirvana without residue; then no matter how he practices austerities, it is not the practice that perpetuates the Buddha-seed, and the benefit to living beings will in the end have its limit. This is his second inferiority.

In sum, prajñā is the Buddha-wisdom and therefore the Buddha-seed; hence it is bound up with the life-vein of the Three Jewels. How much more so this Diamond Prajñā, which has little text and much meaning, unfolding the purport point by point to the very bottom. If one cannot have faith in this sutra that does not turn back, then one’s view is not thorough. How then can one’s compassion, vows, and practice be ultimately perfect? And since one cannot have faith that does not turn back, one naturally cannot receive, uphold, and explain it, nor widely propagate it. Then the ultimate meaning of the Buddhadharma is not clear, and the Buddha-seed is in danger of being cut off. The implications here are extremely grave. How then could one whose faith does not turn back be matched by one who knows only long kalpas of austerities! The World-Honored One did not say this to mean that austerities should not be practiced. He makes clear that one who knows only austerities and lacks right wisdom cannot accomplish ultimate enlightenment and cannot perpetuate the Buddha-seed. Whereas one whose faith does not turn back and who propagates this sutra can not only keep the Buddha-seed unbroken, but also, not attaching to emptiness or existence, can practice such austerities with ease. What the latter can do, the former cannot; what the former can do, the latter can also do. Which then is superior needs no lengthy argument.

From this one may awaken to the fact that though the two gates of contemplation and practice are equally important, the wisdom of contemplation is the master. This is why prajñā is called the mother of all pāramitās. One may further awaken to the fact that though the wisdom of contemplation is the master, that wisdom must be seen in actual practice (throughout the sutra giving is always spoken of together with non-abiding), which makes this meaning clear. This is why prajñā cannot exist apart from the pāramitās. Therefore all Buddhas and all great Bodhisattvas, though they take the samādhi of great emptiness as ultimate, nonetheless in the very midst of blazing manifestation that is the samādhi of great emptiness. It is not that they do nothing at all and sit within a great void. If it were so, it could not be called the samādhi of great emptiness. Why so? Because great emptiness empties even emptiness; it is absolute emptiness, not relative emptiness. This meaning is crucial — it is precisely the essence of prajñā. You must understand it thoroughly and be clear about it thoroughly.

Above, the sutra’s merit has been compared and displayed four times, each surpassing the last. You should know this does not mean that the sutra’s meaning differs so vastly from beginning to end; it truly shows that faith and understanding differ in depth. This meaning has been stated before, but it is of great importance, and I fear some have not heard it. Moreover, this present comparison is added. Let me now make it clear together with the previous three.

For instance, the first time, in the passage on producing faith, the surpassing is displayed by the giving of the treasures of one great chiliocosm. That was spoken of one who can produce a mind of faith taking this as real, and even of one who produces a single thought of pure faith. It makes clear that one who already knows to turn toward Buddha-wisdom thereby inherits the Buddha’s family estate; planting a surpassing cause, one will surely win a surpassing fruit. In the future one will become more than a single Brahma Heaven king.

The second time, at the beginning of the passage on opening understanding, the surpassing is displayed by the giving of the treasures of immeasurable great chiliocosms. That was said after the passage on “one should produce a pure mind.” It was spoken of one who accomplishes the foremost and most rare Dharma. It makes clear that one who can believe and understand to this degree benefits both self and others, and has already accomplished the Dharma of supreme bodhi; hence there is great hope. Thus his merit exceeds the former by an immeasurable factor. The accomplishment spoken of here does not mean accomplishing supreme bodhi; it means accomplishing that Dharma, that is, having already understood it and practiced it. This must not be misunderstood.

The third time, in the passage on opening understanding, the surpassing is displayed by the giving of bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. That was said after the clarification of how to receive and uphold it, to make clear that if one can thus believe, understand, uphold, and teach, then one’s practice goes still deeper into the essentials. Why so? Because one not only knows how to subdue afflictions but also knows how to cut them off, and may hope to realize the dharma-body. Hence the surpassing is not displayed by the giving of the seven treasures of outer wealth, but by the giving of bodies and lives, which is inner wealth.

Now the fourth time, the surpassing is displayed by the giving of countless lives over countless kalpas of long duration. That is said after the passage on deeply understanding the purport and on the method of self-realization. It makes clear that one who can have faith that does not turn back need not undergo long austerities, but can realize what I have realized, just so. Why so? Above, one still could not practice each thing in accordance with the Dharma; now, one’s faith does not turn back, which means one practices each thing in accordance with the Dharma. How can one practice each thing in accordance with the Dharma? Because one has already opened the wisdom of understanding and knows that it cannot be otherwise; hence one can make one’s mind firm and practice without transgressing — one has already turned from dust and joined with enlightenment. Such a one is precisely what is called “one who, at the very moment of first arousing the mind, immediately accomplishes perfect enlightenment.” (See the Avatamsaka Sutra.) He then possesses the qualification to accomplish supreme perfect enlightenment. Hence the text below says: he bears the Tathagata and will surely attain bodhi. Therefore though he is still an ordinary being, his merit already surpasses that of the Bodhisattva of long kalpas of austerities. You should know that the World-Honored One’s thus going from shallow to deep and comparing and displaying four times is intended to make people understand that whatever degree of faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding one has, one has a corresponding degree of merit; the so-called effort is never spent in vain. Yet the purpose centers on faith that does not turn back. Why so? Because if one does not arouse the determined mind and practice each thing in accordance with the teaching, one cannot bear the Tathagata and cannot fulfill the World-Honored One’s original intent in teaching the sutra. Hence all students should have faith that does not turn back, not only in the first half, where non-abiding is made clear in terms of objects, but also in the second half, where non-abiding is made clear in terms of the mind. Only thus does one accord with the World-Honored One’s purpose in speaking this most full display of the sutra’s merit and this faith that does not turn back. Hence it was said above that it is merely occasioned by the text above and takes the textual convenience to expound it. How could it be spoken solely for the first half? One should know it in this way.

Consider that this great section is specially proclaimed after all the meanings above have been concluded. At its end it says: the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable. These two statements both conclude the first half and give rise to the second half. One can see that the purport throughout is one continuous whole. And could the three surpassings displayed in between — teaching and meaning, causal arising, and bearing — together with merits such as producing blessing and erasing offenses, be said to belong only to the first half and to have nothing to do with the second? There is no such principle. Then it is clear that everything spoken in this one great section runs through the entire sutra. (The end of the second half says: one should thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand all dharmas, and not produce dharma-marks. This precisely echoes faith that does not turn back.)

Someone may ask: is faith that does not turn back the same as the “accomplishment of faith and arousing of the mind” in the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, or different? Answer: in terms of stage, they are not the same; in terms of arousing the mind, they are not different. You should know that the Treatise speaks of one in the ten stages of faith who has accomplished the cultivation of faith and arouses the determined mind, thereby entering the first abiding. The first abiding is a sage’s stage. Here it is merely the first arousing of a determined faith to practice according to the sutra; how could the root of faith already be accomplished? Not yet accomplished, one is still an ordinary being. One a sage, one an ordinary being — far apart indeed. Hence it is said that in terms of stage they are not the same. Nevertheless, the determined mind aroused by one who has accomplished faith includes three minds. First, the straightforward mind, because it rightly recollects the Dharma of suchness. Second, the deep mind, because it delights in gathering all good practices. Third, the mind of great compassion, because it wishes to pull all living beings out of suffering. Now the person whose faith does not turn back believes that when the mind of faith is pure, true appearance is produced, and believes that one should produce a pure mind — is this not the straightforward mind that rightly recollects suchness? He further believes in benefiting all living beings, in transcending both emptiness and existence, and in practicing the six pāramitās of giving — is this not the deep mind that delights in gathering all good practices and the mind of great compassion that pulls beings out of suffering? (The six pāramitās and ten thousand practices are the delight in gathering all good practices; benefiting all is pulling out suffering.) Hence it is said that in terms of arousing the mind they are not different. Why should an ordinary being’s arousing of the mind equal a sage’s stage? For no other reason than that he has received from our original teacher the family treasure handed down. One can see that this sutra is truly the great white ox-cart; riding it, one will without doubt go straight to the treasure place. The above was said because I feared some might see the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith and fall into misunderstanding; hence I have specially cited it and made it clear.

There is something further that must not go unknown. The contemplation and practice of this sutra are utterly perfect and sudden. If one can truly understand the purport deeply and have faith that does not turn back, then one is without doubt of perfect and sudden capacity. And a person of perfect and sudden capacity is one in whom a single stage includes all stages; that is, one cannot fix a definite position to discuss him. For he has already opened the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision; not only can the faith he first arouses equal the mind aroused by a Bodhisattva of the first abiding, he can leap straight in and become a Buddha on the spot. It depends only on whether the person himself never turns back to the end and takes up the burden; then he will surely attain supreme bodhi.

Within faith that does not turn back there are already the straightforward mind, the deep mind, and the mind of great compassion. You should know that these three minds are precisely the three categories of pure precepts. For generating the mind while transcending appearances, by rightly recollecting suchness, is naturally free of all faults; hence the straightforward mind is the precept of restraining discipline. Transcending appearances while practicing the six pāramitās of giving, delighting in gathering all good practices — hence the deep mind is the precept of gathering good dharmas. Practicing giving for the benefit of all living beings, to pull out all suffering — hence the mind of great compassion is the precept of benefiting living beings. From this one may awaken to the reason why the beginning of the sutra says that those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit can produce faith in these chapters and sentences and take them as real. For upholding the precept of restraining discipline can arouse the straightforward mind; upholding the precept of gathering good dharmas can arouse the deep mind; upholding the precept of benefiting living beings can arouse the mind of great compassion. And cultivating merit in turn helps arouse the deep mind and the mind of compassion. Then it is all the more clear that to have faith in this sutra that does not turn back, one must certainly begin with upholding the precepts and cultivating merit. Furthermore, the three minds being complete, one can accomplish the three virtues and the three bodies. For the straightforward mind that rightly recollects suchness can cut off affliction and realize the truth; hence it is the virtue of severance and accomplishes the dharma-body. The deep mind that delights in gathering all good practices, because it possesses right wisdom, can delight in gathering; and having gathered good practices, it will surely win surpassing reward; hence it is the virtue of wisdom and accomplishes the reward-body. The mind of great compassion that pulls out all suffering widely binds all conditions and does not forsake living beings; hence it is the virtue of grace and accomplishes the manifestation-body. Faith that does not turn back accomplishes such various merits — how surpassing must its blessing be! Hence the text below says: he bears the Tathagata, will surely attain bodhi; the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable.

(K) Next, selecting the essential and explaining separately. This is in three parts: (L) first, making it clear in terms of teaching and meaning; next, making it clear in terms of causal arising; third, making it clear in terms of bearing.
(L) First, making it clear in terms of teaching and meaning.
“Subhuti, in brief, this sutra has merit that is inconceivable, that cannot be weighed or measured, and that is boundless.”

For one whose faith does not turn back and who practices in accordance with the teaching, his merit surpasses that of the Bodhisattva of long kalpas of austerities. On what ground? Its essential points may be summed up in three, explained in order; hence “in brief.” This sentence runs through the two sections below on causal arising and on bearing.

“Inconceivable” refers to the dharma-body; the dharma-body is the essence. The essence of the nature is empty and quiescent, beyond the mark of names, beyond the mark of speech, beyond the mark of mental activity. Hence one must transcend appearances and realize it for oneself. The so-called “the path of words is cut off (inconceivable in speech), the sphere of mental activity is extinguished (inconceivable in thought)” — hence “inconceivable.” In this sutra, all passages making clear the transcending of appearances and thoughts and the dispelling of everything are for the sake of this. “Cannot be weighed or measured” refers to the reward-body and the manifestation-body; reward and manifestation are mark and function. Having realized the dharma-body, reward and manifestation appear: the reward-body is as tall as Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, with immeasurable marks and excellences, each mark and excellence having immeasurable radiance, beyond what words can describe (cannot be weighed); the manifestation-body follows forms through the six paths, transforming inconceivably, beyond what ordinary feeling can fathom (cannot be measured). Hence “cannot be weighed or measured.” In this sutra, all passages making clear giving, the six pāramitās, and the benefiting of living beings are for the sake of this. The three greatnesses of essence, mark, and function are inherently complete in the nature. Hence one should neither attach to marks nor destroy marks, and only then can there be essence and function. In this sutra, all passages making clear non-attachment to the two extremes, the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, the double cultivation of merit and wisdom, and the union of compassion and wisdom are for the sake of this. This is viewing the two phrases “inconceivable” and “cannot be weighed or measured” together in order to make the meaning clear.

These two phrases having made clear the principle of the nature, the text continues with “boundless” to make clear practice in matters. “Boundless” is the meaning of transcending the four propositions. Not only are the two extremes of existence and non-existence transcended, the two extremes of both-existence-and-non-existence and neither-existence-nor-non-existence are also transcended; this is what is called boundless. When extreme views are utterly absent, the middle way is of itself perfect. This is why the whole sutra takes the two words “non-abiding” as its sole purport. “Merit” means leaping straight in; “virtue” means essence and function both fully manifest. For the teaching and meaning of this sutra is the mutual fusion of principle and practice, the non-duality of nature and cultivation, able by the practice of leaping straight in to accomplish the virtue of the nature in which essence and function are both fully manifest. Hence it is said that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit. The above explains boundless merit in terms of self-cultivation. Yet these four words also include benefiting others; for benefiting both self and others is the Bodhisattva’s path. The dharma-body pervades the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is boundless — how much more the dharma-body! The reward-body’s marks and radiance are immeasurable and boundless. The manifestation-body appears according to conditions with wondrous response in no fixed direction, and “no fixed direction” also means boundless. The three bodies being boundless, they can fill the boundless dharma-realm to save living beings. It means that the teaching and meaning of this sutra can cause people to accomplish the three bodies whose essence and function are boundless, in order to benefit boundless living beings (merit) and together realize supreme bodhi (virtue). And again, benefiting and realizing from one to another, their merit is likewise boundless. One whose faith does not turn back, having practiced in accordance with the teaching, will surely attain such merit. This is the first reason his blessing surpasses that. “The teaching and meaning surpass” is spoken in terms of the sutra. If spoken in terms of the person, it should be said that “the perfuming surpasses.”
(L) Next, making it clear in terms of causal arising.
“The Tathagata speaks it for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle mind, and speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind.”

“Condition” means the opportune circumstance; “arising” means coming into being. It says that the arising of the teaching and meaning arises from the opportune circumstance, making clear that the Dharma must match the capacity.

“Arouse” means to arouse the mind. “Great Vehicle” is the Bodhisattva vehicle. “Supreme vehicle” is the Buddha vehicle. The teaching and meaning of the Great Vehicle may be either perfect or distinct, either sudden or gradual. The teaching and meaning of the Buddha vehicle is solely perfect and sudden. To arouse the Great Vehicle is to arouse the mind that practices the Bodhisattva path; to arouse the supreme vehicle is to arouse the mind that perpetuates the Buddha-seed. This makes clear that this sutra is spoken for such people. In terms of teaching and meaning, the meaning of the first half of this sutra is not entirely perfect and sudden; the meaning of the second half is exclusively perfect and sudden. And the first half’s not being entirely perfect and sudden does not mean that some of it is perfect and sudden and some is not; rather, within a single phrase both meanings are often present. Hence I said before: the shallow see the shallow, the deep see the deep, according to each person’s understanding. This is the World-Honored One’s skill in teaching and his painstaking care in leading step by step. Hence the two phrases “speaks it for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle mind” and “speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind” contain two meanings. First, it makes clear that what is spoken comprises these two kinds of teaching and meaning. Second, it makes clear that it is spoken for those who arouse these two kinds of mind. The word “Tathagata” makes clear that it flows forth freely from the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, and that every sentence transmits the mind.

Since the Tathagata speaks it for those who arouse the mind in this way, then one whose faith does not turn back and who practices in accordance with the teaching may be known to have aroused such a mind, to have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to be perpetuating the Buddha-seed. This is the second reason his blessing surpasses that. “The causal arising surpasses” is spoken from the side of the teacher. If spoken from the side of the one who does not turn back, then it is that the arousing of the mind surpasses and the capacity surpasses.
3. (L) Making it clear in terms of bearing. This is in two parts: (C) first, the direct display; next, the reverse display.
(C) First, the direct display.

“If there be a person who can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and widely explain it to others, the Tathagata will fully know such a person and fully see such a person, and he will accomplish merit that is immeasurable, cannot be weighed, is without bound, and is inconceivable. Such people will bear the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”

In the circulating editions there is a word “attain” before “accomplish.” The sutra texts copied in the Tang dynasty do not have it, nor do the Tang and Song commentaries contain the meaning of such a word. This is enough to prove that it was added by people of the Ming dynasty or later. The intention of the one who added it must have been that a person who has only just aroused the mind could hardly accomplish it already; he could only attain the accomplishment in the future. Suspecting an omission, he therefore added it. He did not realize that the accomplishing of merit spoken of here refers to bearing the Tathagata, not to becoming a Tathagata already. The sutra’s meaning is precisely that bearing the Tathagata is the greatest reason his blessing surpasses that. If this bearing were not yet accomplished, then there would be no reason for his surpassing. Why so? The reason an ordinary being who has only just aroused the mind and begun to practice surpasses that Bodhisattva of long kalpas of austerities is that he arouses the mind that perpetuates the Buddha-seed and practices the conduct that perpetuates the Buddha-seed. “Bears the Tathagata” precisely makes clear that he can perpetuate the Buddha-seed. If this were not yet accomplished, how could he be said to surpass? Moreover, the above explanation that the teaching and meaning surpass and the causal arising surpass serves as the premise for bearing surpassing. For because the teaching, meaning, and causal arising all surpass, therefore one whose faith does not turn back and who practices in accordance with the teaching thereby bears the Tathagata. If the merit of bearing still awaited the future, then he would not have received the perfuming of the surpassing teaching and meaning, and would not fit the qualification of the surpassing causal arising — this would be clear. Then the words above about hearing this sutra and having faith that does not turn back would become empty words. And if he truly had faith that does not turn back and yet had not accomplished the merit of bearing, where would the surpassing of teaching, meaning, and causal arising be? Then the above words that this sutra has inconceivable merit and that the Tathagata speaks it for those who arouse the Great Vehicle and supreme vehicle minds would also become empty words. The addition of a single word has such grave consequences. It was said before that in reading Buddhist books one must absolutely avoid researching them merely at the level of words. For to research words is nothing but to peer with shallow views and measure with ordinary feelings, and one is bound to harm the Dharma and harm people. Now, seeing that here a word has been rashly added with such grave consequences, there is not only the fault of harming the Dharma and harming people, but even the suspicion of slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma. How fearful! Examining the cause, it is nothing else: the teaching and meaning were not clear, and one pored over words exclusively. Why so? In the mind of the one who rashly added it, he must have misunderstood the merit of “immeasurable” and the rest as identical with the merit of “inconceivable” and the rest above. Hence he thought a person who has just aroused the mind and begun to practice could hardly accomplish it, and so added the word “attain” to distinguish it. He did not realize that although the words here resemble those above, since they are stated in inverted order the principle is entirely different, and the merit differs accordingly — how could they be lumped together? Now he has muddled and fuzzed things to such a degree for no other reason than that the teaching and meaning were not clear. How can the teaching and meaning be made clear? Read the Great Vehicle widely to broaden the mind, diligently cultivate contemplation and practice to dissolve one’s obstructions, and constantly seek empowering grace to open one’s wisdom. By the power of perfuming through such contributory conditions, in time one will of itself become clear. If one grasps at the marks of words and seeks it there, one is like a person entering darkness, forever seeing nothing. This is the essential gate for making clear the Buddha’s principles; hence I do not shrink from saying it again and again.

The phrase “immeasurable” and the rest has a subtle and profound meaning; let me now dissect it in detail. Yet to explain the meaning here, I cannot but restate the gist of the meaning above, so that the two may be collated and more easily understood. Where it is restated, the principle is given in some places in detail and in others in brief; the listener should blend and interlink the detailed and the brief as they appear before and after.

The sentence above, “this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit,” contains two meanings. (1) “Inconceivable” speaks of the dharma-body, which is also the essence. “Cannot be weighed or measured” speaks of the reward-body and manifestation-body, which are also mark and function. These two phrases together speak of the virtue of the nature in which the three greatnesses of essence, mark, and function are complete; it is also called the principle-essence. If the virtue of the nature is analyzed finely, then only the essence of the dharma-body is called the essence of the nature; the mark and function of the reward-body and manifestation-body are called the function of the nature. Because they are the function inherently possessed by the nature, they may be collectively called the virtue of the nature, the principle-essence. Such terms are often not fully understood; hence I take this occasion to say a word about them. “Boundless” speaks of the practice, meaning the transcending of the four propositions. Together with the two phrases above, this sets nature and cultivation against each other. As for the two words “merit and virtue,” “merit” means the practice of leaping straight in; “virtue” means the virtue of the nature in which essence and function are both fully manifest. In sum, it makes clear that the teaching and meaning of this sutra has the merit of the mutual fusion of principle and practice, the non-duality of nature and cultivation, leaping straight in, and essence and function both fully manifest. (2) “Inconceivable” and “cannot be weighed or measured” have the same meaning as above.
