But above they were spoken in terms of the nature complete in the three greatnesses, to set against the cultivation of “boundless.” Here they are explained separately. “Inconceivable” may be spoken in terms of the essence of the nature. “Cannot be weighed or measured” may be spoken in terms of the function of the nature. “Boundless” refers generally to all. Benefiting living beings is merit; nurturing bodhi is virtue. Then the four words “boundless merit” are spoken exclusively of benefiting others. If set against the function of the nature above, this is what is called the function of function. In sum, it makes clear that the teaching and meaning of this sutra has the merit of realizing the essence and raising up function, filling the boundless dharma-realm, benefiting living beings, and causing them to realize bodhi together — immeasurable and boundless merit.

Here, however, it first says “cannot be weighed or measured,” then says “boundless,” and afterward says “inconceivable,” exactly reversing the order above: this is the first difference. And instead of saying “cannot be weighed or measured,” it separates and inverts them, saying “cannot be measured, cannot be weighed”: this is the second difference. Further, it not only says “boundless” but adds the word “without,” saying “without bound”: this is the third difference. “Inconceivable” alone remains as before. In such places the meaning is exquisitely subtle.

You should know that the three greatnesses of essence, mark, and function are never separate. That which alone is utterly quiescent, beyond names and apart from marks, and which is the root of mark and function, is called the essence. Its utter difference from mark and function is very easy to understand. As for mark and function, the two are divided yet not divided. For the reward-body and manifestation-body are both manifested by the greatness of function inherent in the nature. Precisely because it can manifest the reward-body and manifestation-body, it is called the greatness of function. And the immeasurable pure virtues inherent in the nature, the so-called greatness of mark, attach to the reward-body and manifestation-body and take outward form; hence it is said to be divided yet not divided. This is why the text above says “cannot be weighed or measured” with the two combined. This principle will become clear on a careful reading of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith.

Yet though mark and function are divided yet not divided, they are also not divided yet divided. Hence the two bodies, reward and manifestation, not only manifest different marks and raise up different functions, but the minds aroused when cultivating the cause also differ (the causal practice is the same, but the causal mind differs; this will be explained below and must be carefully discerned). Precisely because the arousing of the mind differs, the manifested marks and raised functions differ. For though the marks and functions of reward and manifestation are both accomplished through cultivating the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices free of appearances, with merit and wisdom complete (this makes clear that the causal practice is the same), yet the reward-body is the fruit obtained by arousing a vast and endless vow, knowing that the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices are, as conditions arise, just empty, and yet able to increase merit and wisdom and reach the far shore, vowing surely to perfect each one. The manifestation-body is likewise the fruit obtained by arousing a vast and endless vow, knowing that all sentient beings are originally unborn, and yet, still clinging in delusion and not awakening, not yet out of the wheel of suffering, vowing surely to save each one. (This makes clear that the causal mind differs.) Because they differ, the text here again explains them separately. And precisely because it explains them separately, one may awaken to the fact that here it is spoken in terms of cultivating the cause, which is entirely different in principle and practice from the passage above where they were combined to make clear that cultivating the cause wins the fruit.

Viewing the meaning stated above, one may know that to accomplish the immeasurable manifestation-body that divides its person throughout the realm and universally saves sentient beings, one must arouse the mind of great compassion that benefits all living beings and pulls out all suffering. Hence this sutra says at its very opening: all living beings without exception I shall cause to enter nirvana without residue and be extinguished; and again: a Bodhisattva, for the benefit of all living beings, should give in this way. Now it says “accomplishes the immeasurable,” making clear that faith that does not turn back is already the arousing of a mind of great compassion beyond what ordinary feeling can fathom. Having aroused such a mind, one will in the future surely realize such a fruit. The bodhi-mind takes compassion as its root; hence “immeasurable” is spoken first.

Again viewing the meaning stated above, one may know that to accomplish the reward-body adorned with merit and wisdom, with immeasurable marks and excellences, which cannot be weighed, one must arouse the deep mind that widely cultivates the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices and delights in gathering all good practices. Hence this sutra says at its very opening that a Bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding in dharmas, and throughout sets giving alongside the transcending of appearances. Now it says “accomplishes the unweighable,” making clear that faith that does not turn back is already the arousing of a deep mind beyond what words can describe. Consider the five hundred years of patience and the affair of King Kalinga: such hard and arduous practices — how could words describe them? Patience being thus, the other pāramitās may be known. Hence unless the mind of great compassion is first aroused as the foundation, the deep mind can hardly be aroused. And without arousing the deep mind, how could one accomplish the mind of great compassion? That is why the sutra first says “immeasurable” and then immediately says “unweighable.” And to put “immeasurable” and “unweighable” first especially contains an essential meaning. For prajñā is the dharma-gate that makes clear emptiness. The sole purport of this Diamond Prajñā likewise lies in “should abide in nothing whatsoever.” Non-abiding is transcending appearances; transcending appearances is contemplating emptiness. Yet the sutra opens by first causing one to save living beings widely and diligently practice giving, which precisely makes clear that the contemplation of emptiness does not depart from actual practice, and that prajñā does not exist apart from the pāramitās; this is what is called emptiness of the first principle. Now this person’s arousing of the mind is likewise so. The mind of great compassion, the deep mind, and the straightforward mind are aroused together, which is precisely the actual practice of what the sutra teaches; hence it is said that his faith does not turn back.

You should know that when the mind is first aroused, one has not yet cut off thoughts and is still within the gate of arising and ceasing. Hence though the straightforward mind, the deep mind, and the mind of great compassion are aroused together, if one only advances diligently within the gate of arising and ceasing in the six pāramitās that do not attach to marks, do not destroy marks, and universally benefit all, then one already accords with the virtue of the nature complete in the three greatnesses of essence, mark, and function, and further becomes the direct cause for accomplishing the two bodies, reward and manifestation. One will not fall into one-sided emptiness, having essence but no function. Moreover, the delusive thoughts from beginningless time can never be removed without passing through affairs and training the mind. These are all crucial points for students of Buddhism, and a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises all unfold this principle. Prajñā speaks of it with particular subtlety. You must understand it, you must practice it accordingly.

Yet while on the one hand, within the gate of arising and ceasing, one actually practices the six pāramitās (the six pāramitās and the rest are all dharmas arising from conditions, hence they fall within the gate of arising and ceasing), on the other hand one should urgently and subtly contemplate emptiness in order to move toward the gate of suchness. Otherwise clinging cannot be dispelled and appearances cannot be transcended. Not only can one not cut off thoughts and realize the essence of the dharma-body, so that the marks and functions of the two bodies, reward and manifestation, have no way to appear (one must realize the essence before one can raise up function); moreover, giving and the six pāramitās practiced while abiding in marks are like a person entering darkness: on encountering an obstructive condition, one will surely backslide, as the section on patience above makes clear. Hence the text immediately continues: “without bound.”

To “boundless” the text adds the word “without”: this is exquisitely essential. Above, “boundless” made clear that the four propositions are all transcended. You should know that while delusive thoughts have not ceased, as soon as a thought arises there is attachment, and where there is attachment there is a bound. The so-called bound, boundless, both-bound-and-boundless, neither-bound-nor-boundless — when a single thought arises, one must attach to one of the four propositions. Hence to be free of attachment one must be free of thoughts. Now it says “without bound,” making clear that one is not yet able to be absolutely without, but can only use the word “without” to counter “bound.” It says that this person is at work on non-abiding and transcending appearances in order to seek realization of the essence of the dharma-body, in which the path of words is cut off, the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, and which is inconceivable. Hence the text continues: “inconceivable.” The essence of the nature is without change or difference; hence this phrase also remains as before to show that it is unchanging and undiffering. Reading “without bound” and “inconceivable” together, this is precisely the straightforward mind that arouses the mind transcending all appearances in order to rightly recollect suchness. The three minds being aroused together, this is faith that does not turn back. Having faith in this sutra that does not turn back and practicing in accordance with the teaching, one then has the merit of benefiting living beings and the virtue of nurturing bodhi. Why so? Because one can practice the cultivation of leaping straight in and seek realization of the virtue of the nature in which essence and function are both fully manifest. Whether monk or lay, man or woman, whoever can have faith that does not turn back will without exception accomplish in this way. Hence it is said: all accomplish merit that is immeasurable, cannot be weighed, is without bound, and is inconceivable. Only by accomplishing the merit of these three minds aroused together is one fit to perpetuate the Buddha-seed. Hence the text continues: such people will bear the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. “Will bear” means “is precisely.” If this were to be accomplished in the future and were not yet accomplished now, how could it be said to be? Viewing all the various meanings stated above together, this suffices to prove that the rash addition of the word “attain” plainly violates the sutra’s intent.

“Bearing” means directly taking it up and being wholly responsible for it. Since it says “Tathagata” and also “supreme perfect enlightenment,” the Tathagata is one in whom the virtue of the nature is perfectly bright, and supreme bodhi is the Dharma realized solely by the king of enlightenment. To allow that he bears these two is to allow that he is one who succeeds to the Buddha’s position and is fit for the Dharma of the king of enlightenment. “Receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting, and widely explaining it to others” has the same meaning as before. The “a person can” above means one whose faith does not turn back. As for “such people,” the word “such” corresponds to the “all” above. “The Tathagata will fully know and fully see”: here there is no word “by,” nor the words “by Buddha-wisdom,” so the meaning of “the Tathagata will fully know and fully see” is like saying that in the constant quiescent light he has confirmed and approved it. The three essentials above — teaching and meaning, causal arising, and bearing — produce blessing, erase offenses, and surpass the merit of honoring Buddhas; nothing is outside them. Though it is spoken within the passage on producing blessing, its meaning in fact runs through the text below; one should receive it in this way.
(C) Next, the reverse display.

“Why so? Subhuti, one who delights in the small Dharma clings to the view of self, the view of a person, the view of living beings, and the view of a life-span; such a one cannot listen to, receive, read, or recite this sutra, nor explain it to others.”

The text of this section, at first glance, seems not very important; in fact every word is important. Its meaning is deep and subtle, and its threads are many and complex. For with this one section all the meanings above become more complete; one can see how crucial its relevance is. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: split open one mote of dust, and a thousand-volume sutra emerges. Let me now split it open point by point.

The sentence “why so” not only continues the previous section; it continues in one breath directly from the section that sets up the simile onward. This is why its threads are many and complex. “Small Dharma” means the Small Vehicle Dharma, and also refers to the incomplete meaning. It is precisely the reverse of the supremely profound sutra. “Delighting in the small Dharma” is in turn the reverse of hearing this sutra with faith that does not turn back. Hence it is called the reverse display: by means of the reverse meaning, the direct meaning is displayed.

“Delight” means to be fond of and to accord with; that is, the reason for not turning back. Because one is fond of and accords with it, one does not turn back. “Clinging to the view of self” is attachment to a self. Once there is attachment to a self, all kinds of discrimination arise in its wake; hence “clings to the view of self, the view of a person, the view of living beings, and the view of a life-span.” This is an extremely severe rebuke of the Small Vehicle. It has always been said that the Small Vehicle has already emptied attachment to self and only has attachment to dharmas remaining. Now it directly rebukes them as clinging to the view of self, which quite dismays the followers of the Small Vehicle and makes them realize how utterly wrong their delight in the small is. This is a true statement, not a harsh judgment. For the Small Vehicle has emptied the coarse aspect of the view of self — the view that takes the illusory union of the five aggregates and the physical body as self — and this is why it does not receive further existence. Yet because it clings to the dharma of the emptiness of self (that is, the dharmas of the five aggregates), it is said to have attachment to dharmas. You should know that since the emptiness of self is not yet forgotten, one may call it attachment to dharmas, and it is no less true to call it an unpurified view of self. This is why it was said above: if one grasps the marks of dharmas, one clings to self, person, living beings, and life-span. Further, clinging to the emptiness of self falls into one-sided emptiness. One-sided emptiness is grasping non-dharmas, that is, grasping non-dharmas as dharmas; this is still attachment to dharmas. This is why it was said above: if one grasps the marks of non-dharmas, one clings to self, person, living beings, and life-span. Hence here it directly rebukes them as clinging to the view of self. To speak plainly: if the mind grasps, who is it that makes it grasp? No one else — the self. Hence whether one grasps dharmas or non-dharmas, it is always clinging to self. This is why it was said above: if the mind grasps marks, then it clings to self, person, living beings, and life-span. It is only that compared with the ordinary being’s attachment to self there is a coarse and a fine difference; how could the root have been utterly purified? The World-Honored One’s saying this is the tender heart and bitter words of a grandmother, warning those who delight in the small Dharma that they should urgently turn from the small toward the great.
Beyond this there is a further deep meaning, in two respects:

(1) Previously the text always said “marks of self”; here it suddenly says “view of self.” Are “view” and “marks” the same or different? Answer: within sameness there is difference. Whether one clings to a view or to a mark, clinging becomes an illness; in this they are the same. But because there is the delusive view that grasps, there is the illusory mark that is grasped. Hence clinging to a view is the root of the illness of clinging to marks; in this they differ. From this one may see that merely knowing how to dispel marks leaves one’s practice still shallow; one must dispel views, and then one’s practice is deep. Why so? Because if the delusive view is not removed, the root of the illness remains, and the illusory marks cannot be purely removed. The first half of this sutra mostly speaks of transcending appearances. Appearances are objects, hence the general section is titled “Making clear non-abiding in terms of objects.” The second half is devoted to making clear the transcending of thoughts. (Thoughts are views.) Thoughts arise in the mind, hence the general section is titled “Making clear non-abiding in terms of the mind.” This is the sequence of shallow and deep in the first and second halves of this sutra. Now, as the first half draws to its close, he takes the occasion to point out the word “view,” in order to show that the sequence of the two halves joins tightly together, and also to indicate to students that practice should advance in order, from the shallow to the deep. This is the first deep meaning of the World-Honored One’s saying “clings to the view of self” and the rest.

(2) To speak in terms of actual fact: all things that stand in opposition have a connected relation. Hence though the first half says only “transcend appearances,” at bottom it is already transcending thoughts. Why so? Because clinging to marks comes from clinging to views; if one does not transcend thoughts, one has no way to transcend appearances. It is only that one who merely knows to transcend appearances and does not go so far as to work directly at transcending thoughts has a practice that is less direct and immediate. Previously this meaning has been hinted at again and again but never plainly stated. For instance, where it says one should produce a pure mind; where it says that when the mind of faith is pure, true appearance is produced; where it says that if the mind abides, then it does not abide; and also the repeated questioning about the four fruits and whether one can form the thought, together with what is said in the request for the name and the method of upholding — all of these indicate the principle of transcending thoughts. Other statements of the same kind I shall not cite in full. Why then was it not plainly stated? Because all living beings, hearing prajñā make clear emptiness, were already frightened and awestruck; if this sutra had said from its opening that one should cut off thoughts and dispel views, how much more would their alarm be! Better to say only “transcend appearances,” leading people step by step into the wonder. Only in the second half does it lay the matter bare and devote itself to making this meaning clear, so that those of dull faculties may not be timid and have no place to begin. That is why the sentences of the first half have a meaning that is blended and all-embracing, capable of being taken deeply or shallowly, according to each person’s understanding. The shallow, though they see only the shallow, by working at transcending appearances cannot reach the bottom, yet thereby they may also beat down no small amount of delusive thought, which is not without benefit. The deep, on the other hand, can still see its depth, and are not hindered from leaping straight in. Now that the first half is about to be completed, the true meaning cannot but be disclosed, so that those of shallow view may not thereafter fear difficulty, and those of deep view may know that what they have seen is not mistaken. It also indicates to students that what is made clear before and after in this sutra is but one single meaning; only the first half is both shallow and deep, while the second half is deep without the shallow. This is the second deep meaning of the World-Honored One’s saying “clings to the view of self” and the rest. From this one may see the skill in his teaching and the compassion of his gathering in.

Since one delights in the small Dharma, one’s capacity and this profound sutra do not correspond. Thus when the World-Honored One was about to teach the Lotus Sutra, five thousand monks rose and withdrew, unable to listen. When the clinging view is deep, even hearing can hardly be received. If one cannot even hear, how much less read and recite. If one cannot receive, from what could one explain? Hence it says: such a one cannot listen to, receive, read, or recite this sutra, nor explain it to others. The above concludes the meaning made clear in this section.

What meaning does the so-called reverse display display? It displays the sutra’s merit. Above it was said that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit; and the two sections on the surpassing of causal arising and the surpassing of bearing were also spoken to display the sutra’s merit. One might say no meaning is left unilluminated — why display it further? Nevertheless, he feared that some, hearing all the words above, might not blend them together, and so would abjectly settle for the inferior and doubtfully block themselves; then though the sutra’s merit is surpassing, they would sit weeping in the corner. The Buddha looks upon living beings as an only child. He urgently wishes all living beings to be able to read and recite, to have faith that does not turn back, to practice in accordance with the teaching, and to bear the Tathagata’s supreme bodhi. Hence he again himself asks and answers, using words from the reverse side to display the purport of the direct side. Though this displays the various meanings spoken above, in fact it all serves to display this sutra’s merit. For the direct display above displayed it directly; this reverse display now displays it indirectly.
The sentence “why so” is the word of self-questioning. The words “one who delights in the small Dharma” and the rest are the word of self-explanation. The question has three intentions:

(1) Question: why does it speak only of the merit of one who can uphold and can teach, and not mention the one whose faith does not turn back? This question arises from having heard what was said in the first display of the surpassing without fully understanding it. One thinks that to be able to uphold and to teach surely means one’s faith does not turn back. But above it was said that one whose faith does not turn back has merit surpassing that, and how much more one who receives, upholds, and widely teaches. Judging from this language, even without upholding and teaching one already has surpassing merit. Yet now, in making clear the accomplished merit, this is alone omitted. One does not know what his merit ultimately is. Hence the explanation is given through “one who delights in the small Dharma” and the rest. If one knows that one who delights in the small Dharma cannot listen to, receive, or explain this sutra, then one may know that whoever delights in this sutra will surely be able to uphold and to teach — that is clear. You should know that when it was said above that one whose faith does not turn back has merit surpassing that, it is because he has aroused the determined mind to uphold and teach; hence the very arousing of the mind surpasses. If he could not uphold and teach, how could it be said that his faith does not turn back? When it was said above “how much more,” it made clear that one who arouses the mind to uphold and teach already has surpassing merit; how much more one who has already upheld and taught — surely he has surpassing merit! It does not mean that arousing the mind and upholding-and-teaching have different merit. Thus although the section above spoke only of the merit of one who can uphold and can teach, it has already included the merit of arousing the mind. This explanation centers on the phrase “delights in the small Dharma.” To display the meaning thus teaches people that they should arouse the mind and practice according to the sutra. Then at the very moment this mind is aroused, one is bearing the Tathagata’s supreme bodhi. For what the sutra teaches is the very heart-essence of becoming a Buddha. Compared with those who delight in the small Dharma, how could the measure of their accomplishment be mentioned in the same breath?

(2) Question: this sutra is exceedingly profound, hard to understand and hard to practice. Why is it that, on hearing this sutra, one can have faith that does not turn back and receive, uphold, and explain it? This question arises from having heard above that it is spoken for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle mind and for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind; one cannot help but shrink back. One thinks that such capacity is rare and hard to meet; though the World-Honored One wishes to transmit the heart-essence, what can he do if the right person is hard to find? Hence the explanation is given through “listen to, receive, read, and recite” and the rest. If one knows that the inability to listen, receive, read, and recite comes from fitting into the small Dharma, then one knows that to seek to fit into the great Dharma there is nothing but listening, receiving, reading, and reciting. For to open wide a perfect understanding is truly not easy. Better to listen often to the explanations of those who understand deeply; this can achieve twice the result with half the effort. Though for a time one may not be able to enter deeply, still by listening and receiving a single sentence or half a verse the prajñā-seed has been planted. Gaining the power of the perfuming of listening and receiving, and adding to it the power of the perfuming of reading and reciting, once the prajñā-seed sprouts, then without knowing or perceiving it the three minds will be aroused together. Though one’s faculties be exceedingly dull, one can become one of sharp faculties and keen wisdom. The sutra says: the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. Relying on this surpassing condition, what is there to worry about? This explanation centers on the four words “listen, receive, read, and recite.” To display the meaning thus is to open a skillful means for those who wish to enter this gate. Gaining this skillful means, the qualification to bear the Tathagata, though difficult, is not so very difficult. This explanation also carries the intention of encouraging those who can explain. To force oneself on people’s ears is indeed to slight the Dharma; but for one who is willing to listen, one should do one’s utmost to explain it for him.

(3) Question: suchness is without marks. Because all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, it is called suchness. Now, though the three minds are aroused together and one rightly recollects suchness, one still cannot be without thought and without mark. Why then is one at once allowed to be bearing the Tathagata? This question arises from hearing that the Bodhisattva who gives his life throughout long kalpas still does not match in merit; one cannot but doubt. One thinks that the long-kalpa giver of life, though his merit does not match because he lacks the right wisdom of prajñā, is nonetheless already a Bodhisattva; while one whose faith does not turn back, though his merit surpasses because he receives and upholds this sutra, is nonetheless still an ordinary being. Since the root of faith is not yet accomplished, can one be sure there will never be a time of backsliding? Hence the explanation is given through “clings to the view of self” and the rest. If one knows that the failure to purify the view of self and the discriminating mind comes from delighting in the small Dharma, then one knows that one who can delight in the supreme great Dharma without turning back will in the end be able to purify utterly the view of self and the discriminating mind — beyond all doubt. Why so? Because the perfuming surpasses. Having already turned toward suchness, though now one cannot yet cut off thoughts and attain supreme bodhi, one will surely attain it in the future; what doubt is there? (Hence the text below says: he will surely attain anuttara-bodhi.) This explanation centers on the phrase “clings to the view of self.” To display the meaning thus is precisely to show students that if they wish to remove the view of self and other delusive marks and thoughts, it is absolutely impossible unless they believe, understand, receive, and uphold this Diamond Prajñā of total non-abiding. For all Buddhas and the Dharma of all Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-sambodhi all come forth from this sutra. The ancient Buddhas were all thus, and the present Buddha is certainly thus as well. In sum: the World-Honored One, to guard against those who have not deeply understood the purport being unable to thread the above together and so necessarily producing obstruction, spoke this section. From the reverse side it displays various principles, making the meanings above more complete and the supremacy of this sutra more vivid, so that all may enter this gate together, shoulder this task together, and all attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. This is the special purpose of speaking this section. Otherwise, the three essentials above have already thoroughly stated the reason for surpassing; why speak again? Consider that the phrases “delights in the small Dharma,” “clings to the view of self,” and “listening and receiving” come with extreme abruptness; from this one may awaken to the fact that these phrases must have a deep connection with what was said above. If one regarded this section as still spoken merely to make clear that his merit surpasses, then these phrases could not be each word incisive and every one of them have its place; and why would the World-Honored One have spoken them thus?
3. (K) Concluding by displaying the sutra’s supremacy.

“Subhuti, wherever this sutra may be, in every place, all the worlds of gods, humans, and asuras should make offerings to it. You should know that such a place is a stupa; all should revere it, bow to it, walk around it in reverence, and scatter flowers and incense there.”

“Wherever it may be, in every place” is like saying “no matter where.” Yet instead of saying “no matter where,” it says “wherever it may be, in every place,” which carries the meaning that it should be propagated everywhere and is present in all places. “All the worlds”: “world” in the temporal sense refers to a generation, thirty years making one generation; “world” in the spatial sense refers to boundaries. Hence “worlds” is like saying “the world.” To say “all” worlds means pervading the dharma-realm and reaching to the end of the future. Gods, humans, and asuras are the three good paths. To speak of the three good paths implies the three evil paths. To speak of gods and asuras implies the eight classes of beings. It means that throughout the dharma-realm and to the end of the future, all gods, dragons, and the eight classes, the four kinds of birth and the six paths, should protect and uphold it. Offerings are the expression of that protection. “Should make offerings” has a deeper meaning than the earlier words “all should make offerings.” “All should” makes clear that every single living being ought to make offerings. “Should” makes clear that making offerings is the duty of all living beings; not to do so is what should not be. “Is a stupa” also has a deeper meaning than the earlier “like a Buddha’s stupa or shrine.” What was said before was still that the sutra is the sutra and the stupa is the stupa, only that they should be regarded as equal. Now it makes clear that the sutra itself is the stupa. This has the same meaning as the earlier words: wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha, and one should respect it as one would a venerable disciple. For a stupa must contain relics, or images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sage-monks; hence to say that wherever the sutra is, there is a stupa, means that this sutra is bound up with the life-vein of the Three Jewels. Furthermore, relics are the Buddha’s bones, that is, the reward-body. Images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sages serve to let living beings gaze and pay reverence and arouse faith, and their function is the same as the manifestation-body. And the sutra is the dharma-body. Hence to say that wherever the sutra is there is a stupa also makes clear that this sutra can accomplish the three virtues and manifest the three bodies. All these are the surpassing merit of the sutra, hence the section is titled “Concluding by displaying the sutra’s supremacy.” Because it has such surpassing merit, all living beings should do their utmost to propagate it, so that this sutra may be present everywhere. Hence wherever the sutra is, all the worlds of gods, humans, and asuras should make offerings to it. Moreover, a stupa must stand in a high and prominent place. The purpose of erecting a stupa is to make it conspicuous, so that the many may hear and see it and arouse faith. Now it says, “you should know that such a place is a stupa,” which teaches one to know to make this sutra conspicuous and to propagate this sutra. The phrase “should make offerings” is the general statement. “Is a stupa” explains the reason it should be offered to. “Revere it, bow to it,” and the rest separately make clear the manner of offering. What is that manner? All should purify the three karmas.

The two words “revere” and “respect” are both the master and the general. To revere is to be devout, that is, to devote one’s whole mind in surrender. For of the three karmas, the karma of mind is the master. If one merely bathes the body and cleanses the mouth, while delusive thoughts run wild and one cannot be of one mind, what purity is there? Hence one should first gather the mind into one and not let it race outward; this is called reverence. Only with reverence can there be purity. That reverence is the master means that reverence expresses the devotion of the karma of mind, and hence is the master of the three karmas. “Bowing” — joining the palms, touching the head to the ground, and the like — expresses the devotion of the karma of body. Walking around the sutra in reverence is also a form of bowing. While walking around, one may invoke the holy name or the sutra’s title, or chant in Sanskrit melody and praise the merit; this expresses the devotion of the karma of speech. One may also bow and walk around, both expressing the karma of body. “Scattering flowers and incense”: in ancient India, flowers or powdered incense were often held and tossed into the air with one hand as a sign of respect. In our country, flowers are mostly placed in vases and incense burned in censers, which is likewise a way of expressing respect. When scattering flowers and incense, one must add praise. Just as today when offering incense one must sing the incense praise, and in repentance ceremonies one holds flowers and incense in hand and sings aloud, “May this cloud of flowers and incense…” This expresses the devotion of the karma of speech. Body, speech, and mind — all three karmas should be devout, to express reverence. Hence reverence is the general.

That offerings always use flowers and incense has a deep meaning. Flowers express adornment, and hence Buddhist sutras also take them as names, as with the Avatamsaka (Flower Adornment) Sutra. Incense expresses purity, as in the phrase “the true incense of precepts and samādhi.” It also expresses perfuming and thorough penetration, as in “the dharma-realm is perfumed.” In sum, the flower is the cause of the fruit; hence scattering it expresses the planting of the cause of cultivating both merit and wisdom and the realization of the fruit of the adornment of merit and wisdom. Incense is the Buddha’s envoy; hence scattering it expresses the purity of the three karmas and the mutual response between the practitioner and the Buddha.

The place where the sutra dwells is thus surpassing. Then the surpassing of the blessing of one whose faith does not turn back and who practices in accordance with the teaching may be known. If the sutra should be offered to, then one who receives, upholds, reads, and recites it and widely explains it to others may be known to be protected by dragons and gods. The Chapter of Vows and Practices says: “One who recites this vow walks in the world without obstruction, like the moon in the sky emerging from clouds. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas praise him; all humans and gods should revere him; all living beings should make offerings to him.” Reciting the Universal Good Chapter is thus; reciting the Diamond Prajñā Sutra is likewise so. You should know that these two sutras, one expressing wisdom and one expressing compassion, made one’s daily constant practice, are precisely the double cultivation of merit and wisdom and the union of compassion and wisdom, with immeasurable and boundless merit. It was for this that I urged this before.

Conversely, if one slanders this sutra, or despises it, or speaks of it shallowly and wildly, the greatness of that offense may also be known. Viewing the words “wherever this sutra may be, in every place,” one may also know that students of Buddhism should everywhere write it out, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it to others. Otherwise the sutra cannot be everywhere. And in the present age especially one should propagate it widely, so that it may be everywhere. Then everywhere the Three Jewels will bestow their grace and dragons and gods will protect it; then everywhere there will be peace and security. Today this is not easy to achieve. Yet there is one wondrous method. What is it? Arouse the great mind and every day read and recite it for the sake of every place, seeking the eradication of disasters and obstructions. Then not only can every place gain peace and security, but the living beings in every place will surely, without knowing or perceiving it, arouse faith. Such responses are true, not false. Why so? Because there is one true dharma-realm; because all living beings share one substance; because the power of the hidden perfuming is exceedingly great; because this sutra’s merit is surpassing and it is protected by the Three Jewels of the ten directions and revered by all dragons and gods. Moreover, if one can practice thus, one is forsaking oneself to benefit others; one has already opened the eye of the Way; one is contemplating the one true dharma-realm; one is practicing the giving free of appearances that benefits all living beings; one’s faith does not turn back and one practices in accordance with the teaching; one accomplishes merit that is immeasurable, cannot be weighed, is without bound, and is inconceivable; one bears the Tathagata. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, will then bestow the prophecy that one will attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Whether the force of this takes effect greatly or little, quickly or slowly, depends entirely on the strength of the person’s contemplation and practice. What one sits and speaks of today, tomorrow one may rise and put into practice. Good friends, do not neglect these words.

(G) Next, displaying it in terms of erasing offenses. This is in two parts: (H) first, pointing out the cause of being slighted and despised; next, making clear the erasing of offenses and attainment of blessing.
(H) First, pointing out the cause of being slighted and despised.

“Furthermore, Subhuti, if good men and good women who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra are slighted and despised by others, it is because of offenses committed in former lives that they should have fallen into the evil paths.”

The words “furthermore” make clear the meaning of raising the matter again. Though this meaning differs from the former, it arises in sequence from the former. Or, though it does not arise from the former meaning but illuminates it mutually, it must be stated in sequence; in such cases the two words “furthermore” are used to indicate this. If it is merely a different meaning with no relation to what was said above, these two words are not used.

The meaning raised again here is related to the former meaning in three respects: first, in terms of the three essentials; second, in terms of producing blessing; third, in terms of offerings and reverence.

(1) In terms of the three essentials: above it was said, “in brief,” and there followed the three items of teaching and meaning, causal arising, and bearing, to explain the reason his blessing surpasses. Yet of the three essentials, teaching and meaning is in fact the sole principal one. Why so? Because it is when the teaching and meaning are surpassing that causal arising and bearing become surpassing. Since the teaching and meaning are thus surpassing, how could its merit be limited to the producing of blessing spoken of above? It can also erase the heavy offenses of former lives and attain supreme bodhi. Hence this section is spoken again to display it.

(2) In terms of producing blessing: above it made clear that the blessing produced is the accomplishment of merit that is immeasurable, cannot be weighed, is without bound, and is inconceivable; that is, bearing supreme bodhi. Yet bearing bodhi is still the beginning; realizing bodhi is the ultimate. You should know that the reason one who accomplishes the merit of bearing surpasses that Bodhisattva is that he will realize it through bearing. That this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit is precisely because it can cause those who believe, understand, receive, and uphold it to realize supreme bodhi. Moreover, to realize bodhi one must first dissolve one’s former obstructions. And the teaching and meaning of this sutra is what can best eliminate the three obstructions. It is in this that its power to cause the realization of supreme bodhi lies. In sum, only when the three obstructions are eliminated is blessing complete; only when bodhi is realized is blessing ultimate. Only this sutra has such merit; hence this section must be spoken again to display it.

(3) In terms of offerings and reverence: at the end of the above section “displaying in detail in terms of cause,” it says that wherever this sutra is taught, all gods, humans, and asuras should make offerings. Both the sutra and the person are included in that. The section above said only that where the sutra is, all gods, humans, and asuras should make offerings; though the person is included in the meaning, it is not explicitly shown. Hence this section is spoken again to display it from the reverse side. Knowing that being slighted and despised comes about by chance, one knows that reverence is the norm. How does one know that being slighted and despised comes about by chance? The sutra says “if” — “if” means “supposing,” “perhaps there is such a case.” Is this not coming about by chance? Someone may ask: since one is slighted and despised by others, the dragons, gods, and the eight classes must also slight and despise one. Answer: this meaning is not so. You should know that such a person can have faith in this sutra that does not turn back and practices in accordance with the teaching; above it was said that the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees him, so one may know that he receives the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. Then the dragons, gods, and the eight classes who protect the Dharma will likewise protect such a person as always. Hence one may know that the sutra says only that he is slighted and despised by others without mentioning anything else — how deep its purport! “By” is passive in force; “slight” means not to esteem; “despise” means not to honor. Not to be honored by others is precisely the reverse of “all should revere.” How are they slighted and despised? In a narrow sense, by mockery, slander, humiliation, and the like; in a broad sense, by encountering any difficulty or adversity. “Because of offenses committed in former lives that they should have fallen into the evil paths” makes clear the reason they are slighted and despised by others. Having in former lives committed the karma of heavy offenses, one must have incurred others’ resentment; or though one incurred no one’s resentment, one must have been held in contempt. Such cause, such fruit; this is why they are slighted and despised.

“Former lives” has two meanings. First, it refers to previous births. “Previous births” refers generally to all time before this life, not merely the immediately preceding life. Second, it refers to the time before one began to uphold and teach this sutra; thirty years make one generation. The proverb likewise says that one’s earlier and later conduct are as though separated by a generation. The “this life” of the section below is likewise so: one meaning is this present life, the other is the time after one begins to uphold and teach this sutra. “Evil paths” means the three evil paths: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. That the offenses committed should cause a fall into the evil paths shows their weight. This refers to the five heinous offenses, the ten evil deeds, slandering the Great Vehicle, and the like. “Should have fallen” makes clear that in a later life one must fall; for the retribution of the offense is already fixed — this is what is called fixed karma.
There are three essential meanings here:

(1) Whenever people create karma, whether good or evil, it is the ripened that draws them first. That is, whichever fruit ripens first is the one that first draws one to receive its retribution. Hence this section speaks of one who committed evil in a former life and has not yet fallen in this life, awaiting later lives. This is because in the former life he created good karma and its fruit ripened first; or the residual blessing of many lives of good fruit is not yet exhausted, and the time for the evil fruit to be retributed has not yet come. That is why he has not yet fallen in this life. Yet where there is a cause there must be a fruit. Unless one creates a surpassing cause of another kind and quickly realizes a surpassing fruit, how can the retribution of fixed karma be escaped! As the saying goes: good and evil both meet their recompense in the end; it is only a matter of sooner or later. The sentence “should have fallen into the evil paths” precisely makes this meaning clear. An ancient worthy said: “Ten thousand things you cannot take away; only karma follows the body.” This says that all things are empty and only cause and effect remain. Viewed thus, what relish is there in human life? It is truly like a puppet playing a part, drawn and manipulated by the power of karma within a dark curtain. Unless one breaks free of the bonds, then entering and leaving the stage, rising to the surface and sinking again, one plays out all joys and sorrows, partings and reunions, for the spectators to point at, while oneself has no enjoyment and no end — one does not know what one has come for. Further, viewing what this section says, one may know that in discussing cause and effect one must view them through the three periods of time to avoid error. For in people’s creation of karma, those purely good or purely evil are few. Most have good and evil mixed; since the causes are not uniform, the fruits cannot ripen at once. Hence one must view them through the three periods of time to know their ultimate outcome.

(2) Creating karma is the obstruction of karma. Falling into the evil paths is the obstruction of retribution. And the person’s not knowing in former lives that offenses must not be committed is the obstruction of delusion. Delusion, karma, and retribution are also called affliction, karma, and suffering. Delusion is called affliction because one is deluded about the view of self, and hence affliction arises. Retribution is called suffering as spoken of ordinary beings. It makes clear that the retribution of ordinary beings, though they be greatly rich and noble and even born in heaven, in the end cannot escape a single word: suffering. These delusion, karma, and suffering are all called obstructions. Ordinary beings do not know that these three are all delusive marks and thoughts, and from beginningless time to this day they cling in delusion without awakening. Thus these three obstruct their seeing the Way, obstruct their cultivating the Way, and obstruct their realizing the Way; hence they are called obstructions. Therefore the sole purpose of studying Buddhism lies in removing obstructions. All the Buddhadharma of the Small Vehicle, the Great Vehicle, and the supreme vehicle, summed up in one phrase, is: removing the three obstructions and nothing more. This section first makes clear the three obstructions, as the groundwork for the next section on removing obstructions.

(3) This section makes clear that the power of karma is inconceivable. One who receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra should be offered to by all the worlds of gods, humans, and asuras. Now, because of former karma, he is instead slighted and despised by others. Great indeed is the power of karmic obstruction! You should know that karma arises from the mind. Why does the mind create karma? Because of delusion. Delusion is what is called ignorance. Ignorance is the absence of wisdom. All the dharmas of the Small and Great Vehicles can remove obstructions, but the Diamond Prajñā-Pāramitā Sutra of the supreme vehicle is especially the precious sword that removes obstructions. Why so? “Diamond” means the power to cut, that is, to cut off delusion. “Prajñā” is the name of Buddha-wisdom; when Buddha-wisdom illumines ignorance, nothing remains unillumined. Hence it is likened to a diamond. “Pāramitā” means reaching the other shore. For the arising of delusion is the root of creating karma and inviting suffering. When delusion is extinguished, karma and suffering are extinguished in its wake. The three obstructions being dissolved, the three virtues are perfectly accomplished and the three bodies perfectly manifested. This is what is called attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and so reaching the other shore. Hence merely viewing the title of this sutra, one may know that it is the sutra that cuts off delusion, removes obstructions, and reaches the ultimate. Therefore the sutra’s merit is inconceivable. The next section precisely makes this meaning clear.
